old:
Trade liberalisation — falling tariffs and quotas (China's WTO entry in 2001 transformed its trade); advances in transport and communication technology; the growth of MNCs building global supply chains (Apple, Amazon, Unilever); and containerisation, which slashed shipping costs and time.

Plus the deregulation of financial markets in the 1990s freeing capital flows, and global institutions — the WTO, IMF and World Bank — promoting free trade and investment.
new:
• Trade liberalisation — falling tariffs and quotas (China's WTO entry in 2001 transformed its trade).
  • Advances in transport and communication technology.
  • The growth of MNCs building global supply chains (Apple, Amazon, Unilever).
  • Containerisation, which slashed shipping costs and time.
  • The deregulation of financial markets in the 1990s freeing capital flows.
  • Global institutions — the WTO, IMF and World Bank — promoting free trade and investment.

old:
Domestic firms gain larger markets, imported inputs, skilled labour, economies of scale and foreign capital — but face fiercer competition, costlier skilled labour and fragile global supply chains.

Governments and the economy: growth, tax revenue and jobs on one side; income inequality, exposure to external shocks, and two-way pressure on the balance of payments and inflation on the other. The environment loses: more production, transport, emissions and resource exploitation.

old:
Germany's PPF runs from 150mn T-shirts to 20mn chips; Vietnam's from 200mn T-shirts to 10mn chips — each has an absolute advantage in one good. Opportunity costs: a chip costs Germany 7.5 T-shirts but Vietnam 20; a T-shirt costs Vietnam 0.05 chips but Germany 0.13.

Each specialises where its opportunity cost is lower: fully specialised, they produce 20m chips and 200mn T-shirts — beating the 15m and 175mn made without specialisation — and by trading, both consume beyond their own PPFs.

old:
Opportunity cost of a car: A gives up 80 ÷ 40 = 2 tonnes; B gives up 60 ÷ 10 = 6 tonnes. Of a tonne of wheat: A gives up 0.5 cars; B gives up 10 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.17 cars.

A has the lower opportunity cost in cars, B in wheat — so A specialises in cars and B in wheat, even though A has an absolute advantage in both.

old:
Zero transport costs; perfect knowledge of prices, technology and resources; factor mobility within countries, so resources can switch industries freely; constant returns to scale, so doubling inputs doubles outputs; and no trade barriers — no tariffs or quotas.

Each assumption is a limitation: where transport is costly, factors are immobile or barriers exist, the predicted gains from specialisation shrink.

• Zero transport costs.
  • Perfect knowledge of prices, technology and resources.
  • Factor mobility within countries, so resources can switch industries freely.
  • Constant returns to scale, so doubling inputs doubles outputs.
  • No trade barriers — no tariffs or quotas.

Each assumption is a limitation: where transport is costly, factors are immobile or barriers exist, the predicted gains from specialisation shrink.

old:
For: production at lower opportunity cost raises efficiency and global output; competition lowers prices; consumers get variety; access to bigger markets drives growth, innovation and investment.

Against: dependency on imports for essentials leaves countries exposed to supply-chain shocks; uncompetitive domestic industries shed jobs; gains split unevenly between skilled and unskilled workers and between countries; more production and transport damages the environment; and lower labour standards abroad can mean worker exploitation.
new:
For

  • Production at lower opportunity cost raises efficiency and global output.
  • Competition lowers prices.
  • Consumers get variety.
  • Access to bigger markets drives growth, innovation and investment.

Against

  • Dependency on imports for essentials leaves countries exposed to supply-chain shocks.
  • Uncompetitive domestic industries shed jobs.
  • Gains split unevenly between skilled and unskilled workers and between countries.
  • More production and transport damages the environment.
  • Lower labour standards abroad can mean worker exploitation.

old:
Comparative advantage shifts — the UK's loss of it in manufacturing turned manufactured goods from exports into imports. Emerging economies — the rise of China and India has claimed a growing share of world exports and imports.

Trade blocs and bilateral agreements redirect trade between members — the UK's exit from the EU cut EU trade and raised non-EU trade. And relative exchange rates: a depreciation of the pound makes UK exports more competitive, raising exports and cutting imports.
new:
• Comparative advantage shifts — the UK's loss of it in manufacturing turned manufactured goods from exports into imports.
  • Emerging economies — the rise of China and India has claimed a growing share of world exports and imports.
  • Trade blocs and bilateral agreements redirect trade between members — the UK's exit from the EU cut EU trade and raised non-EU trade.
  • Relative exchange rates — a depreciation of the pound makes UK exports more competitive, raising exports and cutting imports.

old:
The effects hinge on the PED of exports. An improvement lets each unit of exports buy more imports, potentially raising living standards — but if export demand is elastic, dearer exports lose so much volume that export revenue, the current account and GDP all suffer.

A deterioration cuts what exports can buy — but with elastic demand, cheaper exports can raise sales enough to lift export revenue, GDP and employment.

old:
Free trade area (USMCA): members remove tariffs and quotas between themselves; each keeps its own trade policy with non-members. Customs union (MERCOSUR): adds a common external tariff.

Common market (EU): adds free movement of factors of production — labour and capital. Monetary union (Eurozone): adds a single currency. Each step surrenders more national policy control.
new:
• Free trade area (USMCA): members remove tariffs and quotas between themselves; each keeps its own trade policy with non-members.
  • Customs union (MERCOSUR): adds a common external tariff.
  • Common market (EU): adds free movement of factors of production — labour and capital.
  • Monetary union (Eurozone): adds a single currency.

Each step surrenders more national policy control.

old:
Trade creation: trade shifts from a high-cost domestic producer to a lower-cost producer in another member country — efficiency and welfare rise. Trade diversion: trade shifts from a lower-cost producer outside the bloc to a higher-cost producer within it — efficiency and welfare fall.

Other benefits: economies of scale, competition, consumer choice, political cooperation. Other costs: loss of sovereignty, unequal gains between members, and dependency on the bloc.
new:
Trade creation: trade shifts from a high-cost domestic producer to a lower-cost producer in another member country — efficiency and welfare rise.

Trade diversion: trade shifts from a lower-cost producer outside the bloc to a higher-cost producer within it — efficiency and welfare fall.

Other benefits: economies of scale, competition, consumer choice, political cooperation.

Other costs: loss of sovereignty, unequal gains between members, and dependency on the bloc.

old:
Synchronised business cycles, so one interest rate suits all members when shocks hit; labour mobility, so workers can move to where the jobs are; fiscal transfers, so a central budget can support regions a shock hurts; and mobility of capital and finance to follow investment opportunities across the union.

The Eurozone is the reference case — and its strains trace to these conditions holding only partially.
new:
• Synchronised business cycles, so one interest rate suits all members when shocks hit.
  • Labour mobility, so workers can move to where the jobs are.
  • Fiscal transfers, so a central budget can support regions a shock hurts.
  • Mobility of capital and finance to follow investment opportunities across the union.

The Eurozone is the reference case — and its strains trace to these conditions holding only partially.

old:
To protect infant industries until they can compete; strategic industries vital to national security; sunset industries in decline, buying workers time to transition; and jobs in high-employment sectors.

Also to prevent dumping — foreign producers selling below cost to grab market share — to improve the balance of payments by cutting imports, and to enforce environmental and labour standards on what enters the country.
new:
To protect:

  • Infant industries until they can compete.
  • Strategic industries vital to national security.
  • Sunset industries in decline, buying workers time to transition.
  • Jobs in high-employment sectors.

Also:

  • To prevent dumping — foreign producers selling below cost to grab market share.
  • To improve the balance of payments by cutting imports.
  • To enforce environmental and labour standards on what enters the country.

old:
Tariff: a tax on imports. It raises the price of imported goods, making domestic goods relatively cheaper. Quota: a physical limit on how much of a good can be imported, restricting supply and raising the import price.

Subsidies to domestic producers: lower domestic production costs so home firms can compete with imports. Non-tariff barriers: product standards, health and safety rules and administrative procedures that make importing harder and costlier.
new:
• Tariff: a tax on imports. It raises the price of imported goods, making domestic goods relatively cheaper.
  • Quota: a physical limit on how much of a good can be imported, restricting supply and raising the import price.
  • Subsidies to domestic producers: lower domestic production costs so home firms can compete with imports.
  • Non-tariff barriers: product standards, health and safety rules and administrative procedures that make importing harder and costlier.

old:
Their effect depends on the elasticity of import demand — inelastic demand means tariffs barely cut imports — and on whether domestic producers can actually expand to replace them; if not, prices simply rise further.

Then the risks: retaliation from trading partners escalating into trade wars that hurt both sides, and the long-run cost — sheltering inefficient firms dulls the incentive to innovate and lift productivity.

old:
Balance of payments (BoP): records all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world. Inflows are credits, outflows debits.

The current account: trade in goods and services, primary income (profits, interest, dividends) and secondary income (aid, remittances). The capital account: minor capital transfers such as debt forgiveness. The financial account: FDI, portfolio investment and changes in foreign exchange reserves.
new:
Balance of payments (BoP): records all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world. Inflows are credits, outflows debits.

  • The current account: trade in goods and services, primary income (profits, interest, dividends) and secondary income (aid, remittances).
  • The capital account: minor capital transfers such as debt forgiveness.
  • The financial account: FDI, portfolio investment and changes in foreign exchange reserves.

old:
Goods: 260 − 340 = −£80bn. Services: 310 − 250 = +£60bn. Primary income: 75 − 60 = +£15bn. Secondary income: 25 − 45 = −£20bn.

Balance: −80 + 60 + 15 − 20 = −£25bn — a current account deficit. The goods deficit is partly offset by surpluses on services and primary income: always net all four components.
new:
• Goods: 260 − 340 = −£80bn
  • Services: 310 − 250 = +£60bn
  • Primary income: 75 − 60 = +£15bn
  • Secondary income: 25 − 45 = −£20bn

Balance: −80 + 60 + 15 − 20 = −£25bn — a current account deficit.

The goods deficit is partly offset by surpluses on services and primary income: always net all four components.

old:
Causes: low competitiveness (dearer or poorer-quality domestic goods), a strong exchange rate (cheap imports, dear exports), high domestic demand sucking in imports, and structural factors such as a long-term decline in manufacturing.

Since the balance of payments must always balance, a current account deficit (X < M) is financed by a surplus on the capital and financial accounts — and vice versa for a surplus.
new:
Causes:

  • Low competitiveness (dearer or poorer-quality domestic goods).
  • A strong exchange rate (cheap imports, dear exports).
  • High domestic demand sucking in imports.
  • Structural factors such as a long-term decline in manufacturing.

Since the balance of payments must always balance, a current account deficit (X < M) is financed by a surplus on the capital and financial accounts — and vice versa for a surplus.

old:
Expenditure-switching (tariffs, quotas, devaluation) redirects demand towards domestic output — effective short-term, but risks retaliation and higher consumer prices. Expenditure-reducing (contractionary fiscal policy, higher interest rates) cuts overall demand and with it imports — at the cost of slower growth and higher unemployment.

Supply-side policies (education, R&D, infrastructure) rebuild export competitiveness — the durable fix, but slow and expensive.
new:
• Expenditure-switching (tariffs, quotas, devaluation) redirects demand towards domestic output — effective short-term, but risks retaliation and higher consumer prices.
  • Expenditure-reducing (contractionary fiscal policy, higher interest rates) cuts overall demand and with it imports — at the cost of slower growth and higher unemployment.
  • Supply-side policies (education, R&D, infrastructure) rebuild export competitiveness — the durable fix, but slow and expensive.

old:
Floating: an exchange rate system determined by market forces of demand and supply for a currency, with no government intervention — the currency appreciates or depreciates. Fixed: the central bank fixes the currency's value, often pegging it to another currency — the bank revalues or devalues.

Managed: fixed within a range, floating inside it. Market-driven moves are appreciation/depreciation; deliberate central-bank moves are revaluation/devaluation.
new:
• Floating: an exchange rate system determined by market forces of demand and supply for a currency, with no government intervention — the currency appreciates or depreciates.
  • Fixed: the central bank fixes the currency's value, often pegging it to another currency — the bank revalues or devalues.
  • Managed: fixed within a range, floating inside it.

Market-driven moves are appreciation/depreciation; deliberate central-bank moves are revaluation/devaluation.

old:
Higher demand for the currency shifts D1 right to D2 along the fixed supply curve: the exchange rate rises from P1 to P2 — an appreciation.

Demand rises with higher relative interest rates (hot money inflows), lower relative inflation, a current account surplus, FDI inflows, and speculation that the currency will strengthen.
new:
Higher demand for the currency shifts D1 right to D2 along the fixed supply curve: the exchange rate rises from P1 to P2 — an appreciation.

Demand rises with:

  • Higher relative interest rates (hot money inflows).
  • Lower relative inflation.
  • A current account surplus.
  • FDI inflows.
  • Speculation that the currency will strengthen.

old:
Competitive devaluation: when a government deliberately pushes down the value of its currency to make exports cheaper and gain a trade advantage.

The risks: retaliation — rivals devalue too, a "currency war" that shrinks global trade; imported inflation — dearer imports cut consumers' purchasing power; and a heavier foreign-denominated debt burden, threatening financial instability.
new:
Competitive devaluation: when a government deliberately pushes down the value of its currency to make exports cheaper and gain a trade advantage.

The risks:

  • Retaliation — rivals devalue too, a "currency war" that shrinks global trade.
  • Imported inflation — dearer imports cut consumers' purchasing power.
  • A heavier foreign-denominated debt burden, threatening financial instability.

old:
Cheaper exports and dearer imports tend to improve the current account, boost growth and cut unemployment in export industries — the mirror image of an appreciation.

The costs: imported inflation plus demand-pull pressure from rising export demand, and lower living standards as import prices erode purchasing power. Which effect dominates depends on the economy's trade exposure and the elasticities of export and import demand.
new:
Cheaper exports and dearer imports tend to improve the current account, boost growth and cut unemployment in export industries — the mirror image of an appreciation.

The costs:

  • Imported inflation plus demand-pull pressure from rising export demand.
  • Lower living standards as import prices erode purchasing power.

Which effect dominates depends on the economy's trade exposure and the elasticities of export and import demand.

old:
After a depreciation the current account worsens first: contracts fix prices in the short run and consumers are slow to switch, so PEDx and PEDm are inelastic. Only as they adjust does the balance improve through the long run — tracing a J.

The Marshall-Lerner condition: a depreciation improves the current account only if PEDx + PEDm > 1. If combined demand is inelastic, it worsens instead.

old:
International competitiveness: the ability of a country's goods and services to compete successfully in global markets.

Two key measures, both relative to rivals: relative unit labour costs — rising faster than competitors' signals weakening competitiveness — and relative export prices, where higher prices than competitors' usually mean the same.
